title: Hands-on: Three Operator Cases
points: Run one notebook to understand three operator studies.
180 minutes / three short exercises / no coding experience required
note: Open Classroom Labs before the workshop. Participants will run fresh numerical calculations and inspect clearly labeled archived model replies. Use the same notebook for all three cases. If devices are limited, work in pairs: one person runs the cells while the other checks the evidence. The deck uses the IEEE ComSoc theme. The classroom cycle is run, change, check and explain. This expanded edition includes a new L10B replay and a proposed control-room advisory pilot. The scheduled teaching time is 180 minutes; allow breaks outside that total. The presenter affiliations are supplied by the presenters. The new Stanford teaching bridge is an adaptation of general reliability ideas, not a claim that the lab implements those Stanford frameworks. Use the six-page Participant Lab Guide for the exact activity steps.

title: What would an operator ask an assistant to do?
points: Ask for a study: compare allowed options and show the checks needed for a decision.
The assistant returns a reviewable proposal linked to the input data and tool results.
note: Start with the operator’s job, not the model name. Read the illustrative request aloud. Ask participants to name the information they would need before making the study. This is a teaching design for an advisory assistant. The classroom notebook provides numerical counterparts for selected steps, not a live control-room connection.
caption: Illustrative study request and review path. The operator retains the decision.

title: What makes this an LLM agent?
points: A fixed script follows choices written in code. An LLM agent can choose a permitted next tool.
Both can branch and use the same solvers. We must test whether model choice adds value.
note: Use Anthropic’s attributed architectural distinction. A conventional program can contain feedback, branches, rules and sophisticated optimization. Those alone do not demonstrate an LLM agent. A generative model can also just write an explanation. In these records Llama makes bounded choices from an allowed list, receives tool evidence and may select another step. This is narrow agency, not unrestricted autonomy. The default class replays those choices.
caption: Same engineering tools, different source of the next-step choice. Both paths require checks.

title: Llama, Python and the operator have different jobs
points: Llama chooses and explains. Python calculates, checks limits and rejects failed proposals.
The operator reviews the evidence and decides whether another study or review is needed.
note: Llama is the language model, Ollama is the local service used to run it, and the application controls which tools can execute. Our recorded wrappers return schema-constrained JSON choices. They do not use Ollama’s native tool_calls protocol. Python validates and interprets the choice before calling numerical functions. Good JSON formatting does not make a claim physically correct. No classroom cell sends an equipment command.
caption: Roles in the recorded teaching workflow. The classroom route shows saved Llama choices.

title: Stanford example: check before you write
points: WikiChat checks claims against retrieved text before drafting its reply.
Our grid version: run the numerical check before writing the study summary.
note: Stanford connection: Lam’s CS224V introduction, pp.19–20, uses WikiChat to illustrate splitting a response into retrieval, claim checking and writing. Our diagram is an original power-system teaching adaptation. Follow the voltage path: read the current allowance, choose a permitted candidate, calculate its result, check limits and explain the outcome. This is an analogy across domains, not evidence that WikiChat is a power-system controller. Ask pairs to name which step would detect a current violation. The figure shown here is an actual excerpt from the supplied Stanford lecture. Ask the audience to point to the claim-checking or policy step, then identify the corresponding Python check in our lab. We borrow the design habit; the notebook does not run WikiChat or Genie. Their non-grid benchmarks are not electrical performance results.

title: A rule and a tool result answer different questions
points: A document can tell us the limit. A numerical tool tells us how the proposal compares with it.
Keep the source, the measured or calculated value, and the remaining checks together.
note: Stanford connection: the lecture’s WikiChat discussion, pp.17–25, separates finding material from checking factual claims. Apply the habit to a grid study: retrieving a current limit is different from calculating current for a candidate. The displayed 99.604410% value belongs to the separate archived P3 OpenDSS replay, not to the learner’s fresh L2 result. This example supports only that current check under its recorded model. A sentence, retrieved document or citation does not establish full-network feasibility. Treat the input limits as the task policy. A text source describes the rule; the solver evaluates the particular proposal.
caption: Teaching analogy. The number shown comes from the recorded P3 replay, which is separate from L2.
source_label: Monica Lam, CS224V Lecture 1, pp.17–25; recorded P3 current check.

title: Stanford example: tools need clear rules
points: Write down the required inputs, permitted tools, limits and stop rules.
Our lab keeps those rules in Python. A language reply cannot change the limits.
note: Stanford connection: Lam p.40 and the published Genie Worksheets paper emphasize developer-defined workflows and knowledge sources. The published framework uses an algorithmic runtime to enforce a supplied policy, with LLMs used for language understanding and response generation. Our lab uses custom Python functions, not Genie Worksheets. The application analogy is to specify the task and prevent a language reply from silently changing its limits or filling missing required inputs. A passed calculation does not prove that the task description was correct. The figure shown here is an actual excerpt from the supplied Stanford lecture. Ask the audience to point to the claim-checking or policy step, then identify the corresponding Python check in our lab. We borrow the design habit; the notebook does not run WikiChat or Genie. Their non-grid benchmarks are not electrical performance results.

title: Ask four questions about a study result
points: Find the tool result, assumptions, rules and the operator’s next step.
If a claim has no supporting result, leave it unresolved and request the missing check.
note: Lam’s pp.52–53 distinguish verifiable rationale, explicit assumptions, policy consistency and actionable next conditions. Translate these into four plain questions: which tool supports this claim, which inputs and model were used, were the same limits and service priorities kept, and what must the operator review next? Our power-flow, optimization and evidence-binding checks are numerical/software checks. They do not inherit the lecture’s SMT correctness claims. Ask pairs to apply the questions to one L10B explanation and to the full-scope HOLD at L12. We show only the actual public returned reasons, not hidden chain-of-thought.
caption: Grid teaching adaptation of Monica Lam’s accountability concepts, Stanford CS224V introduction, pp.52–53.
source_label: Monica Lam, CS224V Lecture 1, pp.52–53; grid teaching adaptation and Classroom Labs L12.

title: Six terms we will use in the notebook
points: Each term describes one job. The language model chooses among tools that do these jobs.
A passing result applies only to the inputs, limits and parts of the network that were checked.
note: MPC plans controls using a forecast. SAC supplies a proposal from a previously trained controller. MILP chooses whole loads while respecting the stated constraints. WLS finds the state that best fits the weighted readings. Evidence binding checks that inputs and command still match a stored result. Model scope means which network parts and physical effects were included. Also define p.u. as a value divided by its stated base: 1.0 p.u. is that base value. A thermal limit here is a current or flow limit. The objective or cost is the numerical score to optimize after required checks pass.
caption: Plain-language meanings. The detailed equations stay in the notebooks and source guide.

title: Know what is running and what is being replayed
points: Python calculates now. Saved controller weights can make a new proposal. L10B shows old replies.
The blue control-room pilot is a teaching proposal. Keep these evidence types separate.
note: Point to these evidence modes throughout the session. Default classroom cells calculate fresh results without a live language-model call. L10B displays verified historical Llama choices, original reasons and associated recorded results. Changing your L2 or L6 input does not change those old replies. The final control-room diagrams are a proposed teaching design, not evidence of a deployed utility platform. No new equipment operation occurs in any of these modes. FRESH means calculated during the current execution. SAVED POLICY means old weights used for new inference. ARCHIVED ACTUAL LLM means an old reply with its original inputs and timing.
caption: Three explicitly labeled teaching modes used throughout this workshop.

title: Colab is a workbook with a computer attached
points: The notebook holds instructions, code and outputs. A temporary computer runs the code.
Save your notebook copy. After a runtime reset, rerun setup and the earlier cells.
note: Explain the picture before using any interface terms. An .ipynb file is the workbook. The runtime is a temporary computer supplied by Colab. Variables and files in its temporary storage are separate from the notebook file. Saving a copy in Drive or downloading the notebook keeps its text, code and saved outputs; it does not keep the whole temporary computer. There is no need to mount the user’s Drive for this lab. The setup cell retrieves the required source and records. We use a CPU runtime and no live language-model service.
caption: Notebook file and temporary runtime are different. Google Colab FAQ; original illustration.
source_label: Google Colab FAQ: notebook storage, execution state and temporary virtual machines.

title: One notebook covers all three cases
points: Save a copy in Drive. Keep this same notebook open for all three cases.
note: Open https://alaaselim-sudo.github.io/GridGuard-Agentic-AI-Tutorials/#notebooks and choose the first notebook, Classroom Labs. The LangGraph and trace notebooks are separate companions. Keep the slides in one tab and Classroom Labs in another.

title: Get ready in four small steps
points: Open the notebook, save your copy, connect a CPU and run setup.
Wait for Ready. Then run L0 and L1 before starting the three cases.
note: For a paced workshop, run the setup cell first, then run each named lesson cell when prompted. Runtime > Run all also works, but it reveals later outputs before the prediction questions. The default route needs no GPU, API key or LLM download. If setup stops, reconnect the runtime and rerun setup before starting L0.
caption: Setup prepares the runtime. Then follow each named lesson cell with the slides.

title: Run a cell, then read what it returns
points: Find the L heading. Use the play button to run the whole matching code cell.
Wait, then read the table or plot underneath it. Editing an input alone does not update output.
note: Point to the three parts: editable input, run control and returned output. The illustrated input lines are the first two lines of the actual L2 cell, not a complete standalone program. The full cell calls the voltage helper and draws two plots. The runtime remembers variables from earlier cells, which is why we run the lesson in order. If NameError reports a missing variable, return to setup/L0 and rerun the required earlier cells. Do not treat a previously displayed output as the result of a number just edited until you rerun its cell. Use the L labels instead of numerical cell indexes. Later cells need earlier variables.
caption: Teaching illustration, not a Colab screenshot. Input lines match L2; run the full L2 cell.
source_label: Google Colab FAQ; Classroom Labs L2, cell classroom-007.

title: Run L0: choose the classroom route
points: Keep both switches False: new numerical checks, saved controller and archived model replies.
If the data check fails, rerun setup before continuing.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L0–L1; cells classroom-002 and classroom-004.
note: Run all of L0 to import the helpers, configure the plots and initialize the timing record. Keep RUN_OPENDSS=False and RUN_LOCAL_LLAMA=False. These settings skip the optional full-feeder OpenDSS route and local model service. They do not make the calculations prerecorded: L2 and L4 through L9 run fresh numerical calculations or checks, while L12 checks the evidence binding and simulated readback.

title: Run L1: does the evidence still match?
points: Read binding_pass: does the record match the same inputs and command?
Expect True, False, False. Changing the load or command breaks that match.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L0–L1; cells classroom-002 and classroom-004.
note: Evidence binding means matching a checked record to the exact inputs, proposed command and returned result, using content hashes. Treat L1 as a same-content check, not a test that a physical action passes its limits. The first row keeps the request and command unchanged. The next two rows change a request field or command field, so binding_pass is True, False, False. A failed match calls for new evidence; it does not prove the changed action fails its limits. A matching hash also does not authenticate a sensor.
caption: Reference L1 output: only the unchanged request and command match the evidence.

title: Work in pairs and explain one result
points: Predict, run, read, change one input and rerun. Explain which check supports the next step.
One person runs and one checks. Swap roles, then save the inputs and outputs.
note: Participants can add a text cell below an output or use paper notes; no extra software is needed. Each pair should finish with one changed-input experiment that another person can repeat. Explain the result and one limit on the claim. The three cases use different networks and do not form a single utility deployment study. Model scope means which parts of the network, quantities and physical effects the calculation covers.
caption: Record one changed input, one result, the check outcome and the next decision.
